newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ wool processors feel pinch as sheep herd drops.
newsitem.headline: NZ wool processors feel pinch as sheep herd drops.

text.p: Overcapacity of nearly 60 percent in wool scouring in New Zealand's North Island is one reason behind the imminent closure of a large processing plant at Wanganui, its parent company Cargill New Zealand said.

In an industry commentary, which also looked at the market's prospects as the current sales season draws to a close, Cargill general manager Brian Sampson said the declining sheep herd, location and economic factors were also behind scour's demise.
"This is more evidence of how tough the wool business is at present," Sampson said, adding that in spite of improved efficiences, "the economics of operating were still not viable."
Sampson predicted the consequences of a steady drop in herd numbers could continue to have an impact on the industry.
The number of sheep in New Zealand has fallen from a high of about 72 million to under 48 million last year.
"Sheep numbers have dropped by approximately 20 million during (a decade), which means there is that much less wool around -- so there may be further rationalisation," he said.
Latest government statistics show the sheep herd at the middle of 1996 had fallen to under 47.4 million, down nearly 1.5 million in a year, and at their lowest level since 1960.
Wanganui Wool Processors will cease its operations, which include the scour work of cleaning and blending, on June 23.
Elsewhere in the industry, commentators said a very difficult year was coming to a close on a firmer note.
"There seems to be a bit more business around and a better tone to the market in recent weeks," wool trading company Dewavrin Fils' managing director David Nancarrow said.
"This is probably being helped by the general improvement and strengthening in the Australian market over the last month," he added.

Auctions this season have been characterised by softening prices for strong fibres and some firmness in fine grade wools amid clear signals that key Chinese buyers are less interested in importing heavy grade wools than in the past.
The next sale is due on June 5 at Napier where 17,800 bales of North Island wools should go under the hammer.
